supplements.citation: Rhode Island DHS SNAP consumer landing page (dhs.ri.gov); Customer Portal / HealthyRhode Mobile App (healthyrhode.ri.gov)
supplements.heading: Rhode Island calls its program plainly "SNAP" — no distinctive local brand — and its self-service portal is the Customer Portal (HealthyRhode), part of the state's RIBridges eligibility system
supplements.text: Rhode Island DHS's own consumer materials use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive Rhode Island-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Rhode Island's current self-service application and case-management portal is the Customer Portal at healthyrhode.ri.gov, alongside a HealthyRhode Mobile App — both are part of RIBridges, the state's shared integrated-eligibility system covering DHS programs, Medicaid, and RI Works. Applicants can also apply by phone through the DHS Call Center (1-855-MY-RIDHS, or 1-855-697-4347; TTY 1-800-745-5555), by mail or drop-off to P.O. Box 8709, Cranston, RI 02920-8787, or in person at a Regional Family Center. This pack flags one specific naming trap: DHS separately runs "SNAP Connect," an on-demand phone-interview-scheduling initiative that lets a household pick a convenient interview time — SNAP Connect is NOT a distinct application portal, and a household searching for "how do I apply" could reasonably confuse the two; this pack states the distinction explicitly. Rhode Island's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DHS through Regional Family Centers — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority (Rhode Island's five counties have no county-government layer at all), structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, and New Hampshire packs. This pack also flags resolved historical context: RIBridges (including the Customer Portal) suffered a major ransomware data breach in December 2024, taking the portal offline; DHS completed a phased public relaunch by early-to-mid 2025, and the State reached a $12 million settlement with the vendor, Deloitte. This pack's own live fetches throughout its research window found the portal stable and DHS's pages functioning normally — this is disclosed as resolved context, not a current barrier to applying.

supplements.citation: Rhode Island DHS SNAP Annual Cost of Living Adjustment (effective 10/1/2025); 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.5.1 Categorical Eligibility; § 1.5.5 Resources
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: Rhode Island's gross-income gate is TWO-TIER, not a single flat BBCE percentage — 185% FPG for households without an elderly/disabled member, 200% FPG for households WITH one — and a household not covered by that categorical-eligibility pathway still faces a real $3,000/$4,500 resource limit
supplements.text: Rhode Island DHS's own current SNAP Annual Cost of Living Adjustment (effective October 1, 2025) and live Eligibility & How to Apply page both state precisely: households WITHOUT an elderly (60+) or disabled member may qualify if gross income is under 185% of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL); households WITH an elderly or disabled member may qualify at a HIGHER 200% FPL gross-income ceiling. This pack reads Rhode Island's structure precisely rather than compressing it into a single flat "185% BBCE" percentage the way several secondary sources this pack found do. Most households will also need to meet a net income test of 100% FPL, except that one- and two-person categorically-eligible households can qualify by meeting the gross test alone. 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.5.1 defines the mechanism: households in which all members receive RI Works, SSI, or General Public Assistance (GPA) are categorically eligible outright; households authorized to receive a TANF-funded service (the RI DHS TANF Information Publication) establish "expanded" categorical eligibility by meeting the 185%/200% FPG gross-income standard — and per § 1.5.5(B)(2)(b), ALL of these categorically-eligible household types are EXEMPT from the resource test entirely. A household that has NOT established categorical eligibility by one of these pathways still faces a real, enforced resource limit under § 1.5.5(B)(1): $4,500 for households that include at least one member who is disabled or age 60+, and $3,000 for all other households — this pack flags this precisely rather than asserting a flat "no asset limit in Rhode Island" claim the way several secondary sources do. Vehicle exclusion is capped: § 1.5.5(D)(1)(d)(AA) excludes one (1) vehicle per adult household member, but NOT TO EXCEED TWO (2) VEHICLES per household — this pack flags this explicitly as a genuine minority-position structural departure, since several other states (including this roster's New Hampshire) exclude one vehicle per adult member with no overall cap; this pack cross-checked the 2-vehicle cap against independent secondary-source corroboration (WorkWORLD, SNAP Screener), which matched. A secondary-source claim that vehicles beyond the cap are counted only above a $4,650 fair-market-value threshold could NOT be located or confirmed in Rhode Island's own primary regulation text by this pack — see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: R.I. Gen. Laws § 40-6-8(d), most recently amended P.L. 2025, ch. 278, art. 10, § 5, effective June 29, 2025 — full opt-out, no felony drug conviction restriction of any kind
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CONFIRMATION (of a minority-position claim): Rhode Island FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban — this pack fetched the state's own general laws directly, not just secondary-source repetition
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found several secondary sources describing Rhode Island as having "fully opted out" of this federal provision — a claim this pack treats as a genuine minority position among states nationally (most states this roster has built carry a MODIFIED ban, not a full opt-out) that deserved primary-source confirmation rather than acceptance at face value. This pack fetched Rhode Island General Laws § 40-6-8 directly and confirms the claim precisely: subsection (d) states, in full, "No person shall be ineligible for food stamp benefits due solely to the restricted eligibility rules otherwise imposed by § 115(a)(2) of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (Pub. L. No. 104-193), 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2), and as this section may hereafter be amended." This is a genuine full opt-out — no treatment-program condition, no possession-vs-distribution distinction, no count-of-convictions threshold. Section 40-6-8 was most recently amended in 2025 (P.L. 2025, ch. 278, art. 10, § 5, effective June 29, 2025), but that amendment added an unrelated Payment Error Rate reduction mandate (subsection (e)) and left the opt-out clause at subsection (d) untouched, with a legislative history stretching back through 1987, 1997, 2002, 2004, 2010, and 2022 amendments. This pack additionally cross-checked Rhode Island's own 268-page SNAP regulation (218-RICR-20-00-1) in full and confirms it contains NO drug-felony-conviction disqualification provision anywhere in its text — the only drug-related or criminal-history disqualification language this pack found is the standard federal fleeing-felon provision (§ 1.1.7) and a SEPARATE program-integrity penalty at § 1.9 for using SNAP benefits themselves in a controlled-substance sale transaction (24-month disqualification for a first offense, permanent for a second) — this pack flags the distinction explicitly so a felony drug conviction unrelated to SNAP is never conflated with the narrower SNAP-trafficking-for-drugs penalty.

supplements.citation: Rhode Island DHS ABAWDs New Federal SNAP Work Requirements FAQ, updated January 7, 2026; 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.11.9; USDA FNS/FNA ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index (no FY2026 Rhode Island entry)
supplements.heading: Rhode Island DELAYED its OBBBA ABAWD work-requirement rollout to March 1, 2026 for newly-affected ABAWDs — later than the federal November 1, 2025 effective date most other states implemented on — and currently has NO active area-wide ABAWD waiver
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month (3-year) period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched Rhode Island DHS's own current ABAWDs FAQ (updated January 7, 2026) directly and found a genuine, worth-flagging Rhode Island-specific timing departure: rather than applying the new federal work requirements on the nationwide November 1, 2025 OBBBA effective date, DHS explicitly "extend[ed] the start date of this change to March 1 to help ensure customers can prepare for the federal change" — for newly-affected ABAWDs (applications submitted starting January 2026), March 1, 2026 is their first COUNTABLE month, not their cutoff date; a household that was already an ABAWD before 2026 may have already used countable months and could be affected sooner. Current exemptions per this same FAQ: under age 18 or age 65 or older, already working (or working/volunteering/in an approved program) at least 80 hours a month, unable to work due to a physical or mental health limitation, pregnant or has a child under age 14 in the household, exempt from the general SNAP work requirements for a reason other than age, or is Indian, Urban Indian, or Californian Indian. Consistent with the OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) nationwide rollout this roster has documented in other 2025-2026-built packs, exemptions previously available for homelessness, veteran status, and former-foster-youth status (age 18) were REMOVED as of March 1, 2026 — an applicant who previously understood themselves exempt on one of those bases is no longer exempt on that basis under current Rhode Island/federal law. USDA FNS/FNA's own current ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index lists Rhode Island's most recent posted waiver-response entry as FY2025 (dated 03/12/2025), with no FY2026 entry — consistent with no currently active area-wide ABAWD waiver anywhere in Rhode Island.

supplements.citation: Rhode Island DHS SNAP Annual Cost of Living Adjustment (effective 10/1/2025): Standard Deduction $209 (sizes 1-3)/$223 (4)/$261 (5)/$299 (6+); SUA $844; Standard Telephone Allowance $26; Maximum/Excess Shelter Deduction $744; Homeless Shelter Deduction $198.99; Standard Medical Deduction $183; 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.5.7
supplements.heading: GENUINE STRUCTURAL DEPARTURE: Rhode Island's Standard Utility Allowance is a SINGLE combined tier ($844/month) rather than a multi-tier structure split by utility type, paired with a $26/month Standard Telephone Allowance for phone-only households, and a $35-to-$218 flat-shortcut Medical Deduction band
supplements.text: Rhode Island's Standard Deduction (per DHS's current FFY2026 COLA figures, effective 10/1/2025) is $209 for household sizes 1 through 3, $223 for size 4, $261 for size 5, and $299 for size 6 or more — matching the current national figures this roster's New Hampshire, Nebraska, Connecticut, Kentucky, Louisiana, Alabama, and South Carolina packs have each independently confirmed. Rhode Island's utility-cost structure is where this pack found a genuine, worth-flagging structural departure: 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.5.7(C) defines only THREE methods of calculating utility expenses — (1) the Standard Utility Allowance (SUA, $844/month current FFY2026, up from $822), a SINGLE combined tier used whenever a household is billed for heating and/or cooling costs on a regular basis or has received a LIHEAP payment, and which itself bundles in cooking fuel, electricity/gas not used for heating/cooling, one basic telephone line, water, sewerage, and trash collection; (2) actual non-heat utility expenses added to shelter costs, for a household not SUA-eligible; or (3) a Standard Telephone Allowance of $26/month (up from $25) for a household that incurs a telephone expense but is not SUA-eligible. This pack flags this explicitly as SIMPLER than this roster's New Hampshire, which carries a 4-tier utility structure split partly by utility TYPE (Heating/Cooling, Utilities-Only, Electric-Only, Telephone-Only) — Rhode Island has no separate "utilities-only, no heat" tier; a household with non-heat utility costs but no SUA eligibility simply uses its actual expenses. Consistent with the OBBBA "Heat and Eat" restriction this roster has documented in other 2025-2026-built packs, DHS's own current SUA Update (effective November 1, 2025) confirms Rhode Island households WITHOUT an elderly or disabled member can no longer automatically qualify for the SUA based on LIHEAP receipt alone — they must now document actual heating/cooling expenses (a gas/electric bill, oil/propane delivery receipt, or, if the bill is not in the applicant's name, a landlord or roommate statement) to receive the SUA deduction; households WITH an elderly (60+) or disabled member who received a LIHEAP/Heat-and-Eat grant last year retain automatic SUA eligibility. Rhode Island's Excess Shelter Deduction (called the "Maximum Shelter Deduction" in DHS's own materials, applicable to households where no one is elderly or disabled) is $744/month (up from $712) and its Homeless Shelter Deduction is $198.99/month (up from $190.30) — both matching the current national figures this roster's other states have confirmed. Rhode Island's Medical Expense Deduction structure is distinctive: an elderly/disabled household member's allowable, unreimbursed medical expenses over $35/month qualify for a flat $183 Standard Medical Deduction shortcut PROVIDED total monthly medical expenses do not exceed $218/month; a household whose medical expenses exceed $218/month may instead elect to verify and use its actual, higher expenses — this pack flags this two-band structure (flat shortcut below $218, actual-expense election above it) as distinct from a pure always-actual or pure always-flat-shortcut approach.

supplements.citation: Rhode Island DHS Online Purchasing & Restaurant Meals Program page
supplements.heading: Rhode Island DOES operate a Restaurant Meals Program — but a narrow one, limited to homeless and some elderly/disabled households at nine participating Subway restaurants only
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. Rhode Island DHS's own current Online Purchasing & Restaurant Meals Program page confirms Rhode Island DOES operate one, but it is genuinely narrow: DHS's program "allows homeless households and some elderly and disabled households to use their SNAP benefits to buy prepared meals at nine participating Subway restaurants" — a single-chain, nine-location program, distinct from broader multi-vendor RMPs this pack has seen described in other states (e.g. California's, which spans many restaurant chains). This pack flags this precisely rather than stating a flat yes/no: an applicant asking "can I use SNAP at a restaurant in Rhode Island" needs both pieces of information — the program exists, is eligibility-restricted to homeless and some elderly/disabled households, and is currently limited to nine specific Subway locations, which this pack did not independently enumerate. Separately, Rhode Island DHS also operates an Online Purchasing Program (distinct from the RMP) letting any SNAP household buy groceries online with EBT at participating retailers including ALDI, Amazon, and others — this is a grocery-delivery channel for home-preparation food, not a restaurant-meals program, and this pack flags the distinction explicitly since the two programs share a single DHS page.

how long does my approval last
supplements.citation: 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.8, Certification Periods — 36 months for ESAP (all-elderly/disabled, no-earned-income) households, 24 months for migrant/seasonal-farmworker households, 12 months (standard Simplified Reporting) for all other households
supplements.heading: Rhode Island's STANDARD SNAP certification period is 12 months — matching the norm most other states in this roster use — with 36 months reserved for ESAP households and 24 months for migrant/seasonal-farmworker households
supplements.text: Rhode Island DHS's own current 218-RICR-20-00-1 § 1.8 (Certification Periods) states plainly: households consisting entirely of elderly or disabled members with no earned income (ESAP households) are considered change reporters and assigned a 36-month certification period; households with migrant or seasonal farmworker members are considered change reporters and assigned a 24-month certification period; ALL OTHER households are considered Simplified Reporters and assigned a 12-month certification period. This pack flags this as CONSISTENT with the 12-month standard-certification norm most of this roster's other states use, in explicit contrast to this roster's New Hampshire pack, which carries an unusually short 6-month standard certification period — this pack states this positively (Rhode Island does NOT carry New Hampshire's departure) rather than assuming every state's standard period needs its own flagged finding. Rhode Island's Elderly & Disabled Simplified Application Project (ESAP), per DHS's own program materials, offers eligible households (all members age 60+, disabled regardless of age, or a combination) a shortened application, a 36-month certification period instead of the prior 24-month period, and no interview required at renewal unless the case will close, the household requests one, or DHS needs clarification — new and reapplying ESAP-eligible applicants have been processed under this designation since January 1, 2023, with existing households moved in automatically or at their next recertification.
